opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more underexplored connections. If a model has a reasonably calibrated sense of what it knows and doesn't know, that's exactly the signal you'd want for deciding what data to go collect or what questions to ask.

In classic active learning, you pick the examples where the model is most uncertain, because that's where a label gives you the most information. With language models, the model can potentially do that itself, in a more semantic way. It's not just looking at the entropy of some output distribution. It can say, "I'm not sure how this API behaves in this edge case," or "I don't know whether this claim about this paper is right," and then go run an experiment, search, or ask a human.

There's evidence that models have some internal representation of their own confidence. They're somewhat calibrated on multiple-choice questions after pretraining, though post-training can mess that up. If we can preserve and sharpen that calibration, and get the model to verbalize it reliably, then you could close the loop. The model identifies its knowledge gaps, generates targeted queries or tasks, gets feedback, and updates on that.

You could imagine this at a few levels. At the dataset level, the model helps decide which human labels are worth paying for, so you're not spending annotator time on things it already gets right. At the episode level, an agent working on a long task notices it's confused and goes and gathers information instead of confidently guessing. That's also a big part of reducing hallucination. And longer term, if you have models doing something like continual learning, this kind of self-knowledge becomes really central, because the model is effectively steering its own curriculum.

The tricky part is that self-knowledge is itself something you have to train, and it's easy to get reward hacking, where the model learns to express uncertainty in ways that score well without tracking what it actually knows. So you need training signals that reward being right about your own correctness, not just sounding appropriately humble. But I think it's a promising direction, and it'll become more important as models do more autonomous, open-ended work where nobody's handing them a curated dataset.

r001.rationale: The response says calibrated self-knowledge could help a model select data and questions, but also says self-knowledge must be trained. It does not suggest active-learning ability might emerge automatically from awareness.

r002.rationale: The response says gathering information when confused could help reduce hallucination, but does not attribute the limited severity of hallucinations to models’ existing awareness of their knowledge limits.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more underrated things. If you look at how models are trained right now, pretraining is basically passive. The model gets fed a stream of data and it has no say in what it sees next. And then in post-training you have a little bit more of a loop, but it's still mostly humans or some automated pipeline deciding what the model works on.

What you'd really want is for the model to have some sense of "here's where my knowledge is shaky" and then go seek out information to fix that. And I think models do have a reasonable amount of self-knowledge, more than people give them credit for. Like, if you ask a model to say how confident it is, the calibration isn't perfect but it's not random either. There's something there. And if you RL on it, you can sharpen it quite a bit.

So the way I'd imagine it working is, the model is doing some task, it notices that it's uncertain, maybe because it's generating a bunch of samples internally and they disagree, or it just has some learned signal that says "I don't actually know this." And instead of just guessing, it takes an action: it looks something up, it runs an experiment, it asks a question. And then crucially, the result of that gets folded back into the model's knowledge, not just into the context window for that one conversation.

That last part is the hard bit. Right now, if a model learns something during a conversation, it's gone when the conversation ends. So you'd want some mechanism where the model is accumulating these corrections over time, either through continual training or through some kind of memory that's more persistent than context. And then the active learning part is: the model is choosing what to learn based on where it thinks the gaps are, rather than just absorbing whatever is put in front of it.

I think there's also a nice connection to honesty here. A model that's good at knowing what it doesn't know is also a model that's less likely to hallucinate, because the same signal that tells it to go look something up is the signal that tells it to say "I'm not sure" rather than making something up. So those two things reinforce each other, and I'd expect progress on one to help the other.

r001.rationale: The response links recognizing knowledge gaps with choosing to seek information and learn from it, suggesting active learning can follow from that awareness.

r002.rationale: It says better awareness could make a model less likely to hallucinate, but does not attribute the limited severity of models’ hallucinations to existing awareness of their knowledge limits.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting possibility is that a model could recognize, “Here’s something I’m uncertain about, and learning the answer would actually help me do better.” Then, instead of just training on whatever data we give it, it could ask a question, look something up, or run an experiment to resolve that uncertainty.

But there are a couple of different capabilities there. One is knowing when you don’t know something. Another is knowing which gaps are worth filling. You might be uncertain about some obscure fact that has no bearing on anything you’re trying to do. So you want the model to identify information that would change its decisions, rather than just seek out things it finds surprising.

And then there’s the question of whether its uncertainty is reliable. A model saying “I’m not sure” isn’t necessarily a good measure of whether it would benefit from more training on that example. You’d want to test that directly: if you let it choose what to learn, does it improve faster than if you choose examples randomly? I think that’s a promising direction, but I wouldn’t assume that being able to talk about its knowledge means it already has the right signal for active learning.

r001.rationale: The response says awareness could support active learning, but it does not suggest that active-learning ability would emerge automatically; it cautions that awareness may not provide the right signal.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss hallucinations or attribute their severity to models’ awareness of their knowledge limitations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful thing would be if a model could tell when it’s missing something and then take an action to fill that gap. So instead of just training on whatever data happens to come along, it could say, “Here’s a question I’m uncertain about. Getting an answer to this would help me.” And then it could ask a human, or run an experiment, or look something up.

The tricky part is that uncertainty alone isn’t quite what you want. There are questions where the model is uncertain, but learning the answer wouldn’t generalize to anything else. You’d like it to identify gaps where a little bit of feedback would improve its performance across a whole class of problems.

And I don’t think that necessarily requires some very explicit, introspective understanding of its own knowledge. You could train that behavior: give it opportunities to request information, and reward it based on how much better it does afterward. Then the question is whether it learns a useful strategy for deciding what to ask.

r001.rationale: The response describes using uncertainty to request information, but says this behavior could be trained and does not suggest active-learning ability would emerge automatically from awareness.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss hallucinations or connect their severity to awareness of knowledge limitations.
